posts.title: Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do?
posts.text: I'm Senior software engineer in the US (DMV area), with 15y of experience. Worked for Fortune 50+ company and bunch of mid-size companies. Been unemployed for 2y and can't find a job, within those 2 years, I pretty much spent my savings that I've saved through years, maybe have 4-5 months left to support my household. Currently, I tutor math and probably about to start working as manager in pizzaria. In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE. At this point, I have massive gap in my resume that I can't explain to recruiters, I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI, but who cares if date of my last employment is Jan2025. What should I do ? If you have an alternative path (something completely different from SWE or SWE adjacent) that pays "well", I would like to hear.

comments.text: > In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE. I don't know the OP's circumstances. What I am about to say is meant as advice to others and not a criticism of the OP. If you suspect that you may be the target of a layoff, DO NOT SIMPLY QUIT. In this scenario you are a potential liability to your employer. They will almost certainly pay you to leave if they decide to part ways. It is always easier to find a job when you have a job. Maybe you think if there are layoffs and you are retained that it will be a miserable working environment. Fine. DO NOT QUIT. After a round of layoffs you are relatively safe and you can use that time to find another job. It is very likely that layoffs are going to continue as companies restructure because of AI. Have a plan. Keep your wits and hold fast.
comments.author: powvans

comments.text: There's a short comment elsewhere here that says "you need to lie" which basically summarizes it. To expand on that: you need to tell potential employers about your AI-powered SaaS or whatever startup that you've been working on for the past two years, how much you accomplished just by yourself with the help AI agents, how much you learned about using AI effectively, etc. That you just couldn't get enough traction in sales and funding and the area you addressed is now being broadly up-ended by AI, so you are looking for a more regular job On the side you obviously need a demo of what you've built over these two years, but Claude can help with both brainstorming what your startup actually did and building it retroactively. In the process it will force you to actually start using AI for real which will be a nice bootstrap for your eventual real job.

comments.text: I had to get back into the industry last year after 4 years off for mental health and caregiving. I was able to get back in - 2 years isn’t that much. But the problem is the front door in hiring is broken. Entirely. I didn’t receive almost ANY replies from hundreds of sent out resumes - I have household names and big public high scale launches and wins on my resume, but no FAANG and no degree. I got 2 job offers. One was through a manager from 8 years prior who was working at a place. One was a recruiter who found me on LinkedIn. I got engagement when someone physically actually knew me, they were actually hiring, and my skills overlapped. My honest advice is to apply places and try that dance, get yourself in front of people, real people, and mainly 1-1. Work everyone you have ever worked with. If you’ve reviewed their PR, they need to know that you need a job. Be kind and genuinely catch up with them if you want to, but they are your PRIMARY resource to get a job and you can’t let shame get in your way. Corporations in general are BROKEN right now in massive ways and the industry is going through a crisis. It will likely become better but whatever you have to do to survive do it. Finally, it seems like solutions architects seem in demand lately, anyone who can help customers with solutions - SWEs can tend to do well if you have some people skills.
comments.author: taurath

comments.text: Something I expect from a senior engineer is the ability to take a failure without placing blame, and turn it into an opportunity to improve things while also taking actions to prevent the same failure mode from occuring. Gaps on resumes are not unique to you. People have unexpected unemployment for many reasons. If you treat that gap like it's a negative thing, and as you say "explain it", I'm going to think there's something negative behind it. Instead treat it as a matter of fact, then present the opportunities you took in the mean time. What makes someone with a gap stand out to is how they "sell" that gap to me. What did you do in that time to improve yourself, keep your skills sharp, grow as a human being? How are you going to show me that you still have passion and drive to remain in this industry? Also, reframe your thinking. You are not an engineer looking for work, you are a sales person selling an engineer. Take time to understand what qualities in an engineer they want beyond mere skills and experience. For example, you don't sell a used car by starting with "It's been on the road 15 years". You try to appeal to what the buyer is looking for. Do they want an easily customizable sports car, a reliable commuter, fuel efficiency? Hiring teams are buyers, you're the product. There's a lot of other boring sounding, but good advice in this thread, such as networking. Networking should not just be about meeting people who may be hiring, it's also about keeping a pulse on the industry and social engagement beyond just talking within online forums. Go to free conferences, meet people, engage. It makes it a lot easier to interview. Whatever you do, don't lie, and I recommend blocking anyone who recommend you do.

comments.text: This is still the best article I've found on this subject: https://ludic.mataroa.blog/blog/ludics-guide-to-getting-soft... from one of my favourite bloggers, his other stuff is very worth reading. My take on it: the standard recruitment process is completely broken. Don't even start doing that. Sending applications to a job advert is an exercise in futility and will destroy your mental health. It's always about who you know. You have to go find people who are in a position to employ you, and impress them. This isn't difficult. They don't want to interview the stream of idiots that HR have approved any more than you want to jump through the hoops HR think are relevant. They want to employ someone who they know and like. So go to meetups, small business networking events, tech conventions, anything that will attract the kind of boss that you want to have. Talk to people. If you can, present something.

Now 2 years later and I'm a plumber, the demand is good and the work is dirty but rewarding as you help people directly. I'm looking to get into an electrician apprenticeship next year and hopefully one where automation is encouraged to put some of the coding skills I've developed to use because the pay just scales better better and the work sounds more fun. Started coding again half a year ago, helping friends and family with websites and bots. Now even working on some personal apps to replace annoyances I find. I still miss working from home and working together in a team with a deadline, but the trades also have their pros. Good luck OP in whatever you choose to do!

comments.text: > "I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI" Let me give you some harsh feedback. You can't have "learned the AI" and still think coding in C#/.NET/AWS is a valuable skill. It's not; the AI codes better than you. It also codes faster than you can read it. My strategy has been focusing on orchestrating highly automated workflows that can deliver software at breakneck speeds. I only focus on the business domains, security, and software architecture. Try this to start: check out the /wayfinder skill from Matt and build something you could never have in the past. Extra points if it's something you can sell to a small business. A system for your local gym, for instance. Give yourself a single week. Coding is not a job anymore. It has evolved.

comments.text: So there is a path that I would suggest to anyone ranging from just graduated to senior who is struggling to find something. Volunteer somewhere while you are looking for a job. This works for MANY reasons: - it keeps your mind occupied and avoids "doom looping" when interviews don't work out or you are waiting for new interviews - it makes you feel good to help people - there is a strong chance that you will either meet someone who can help you find a new job OR you find some new career path/startup idea you didn't expect You would be ASTOUNDED at some of the crazy things that people do b/c they don't have a tech background but need to get things done. And if you help them, you better believe that word travels fast if you are good with technology and can actually make things happen. You can also be more targeted in your volunteering. e.g. your odds of getting a high paying tech jobs might be better if you volunteer via the church or social organization in your upper middle class town vs a lower income area. But again, you never know where the opportunities are so it's good to try both. In closing, who would you rather hire: - Candidate A that has a two year hole in their resume - Candidate B who spent two years volunteering and has great stories about implementing tech for charity roups

comments.text: Things are pretty tough out there. In addition to empathy, let me try to offer some advice as someone observing industry trends from the outside for a while -- especially in the center of the AI insanity that is the Bay Area: The buzzword everyone is looking for is "high-agency." No, not those agents, but yes, those will be essential. Basically employers want someone who will start something from scratch and take it to the finish line all by themselves. So my advice, which others have echoed here: Build something useful -- end-to-end -- from scratch -- with AI -– on your own -- that you can show off as soon as possible. The key point is, "high agency" is by definition not something you can just put on your resume; It is something you show , not tell. Yes, you need to do this even as you go through the absolute hell that is a job search. But trust me, this will a) help get a much better job, and b) help in the long run throughout and beyond your career. This will be the most valuable skill in the near future. A few other thoughts: 0. Get a $100 Pro subscription. Either GPT or Claude, doesn't matter much, but you do want access to Fable or Astra. The volume and variety of things you can get done in that quota is astounding. Codex offers a free quota with Astra if you want to get a sense of things. 1. Target a domain you are already very familiar with. You can draw on your long experience as an engineer, or any personal interests you may have. Say a Math tutoring web app that your students could use. This will sharply cut down the time to MVP. 2. Being an end-to-end thing, this will necessarily be something multi-disciplinary. Think of it as doing a one-person startup, so you're going to be forced to do everythig: design, frontend, backend, infra, and maybe even GTM stuff like marketing. Yes, you may not know most of these things, and obviously won't be great at them, but with AI, everything will be good enough. 3. This conveniently also helps explain the gap in your resume. Nobody needs to know you did this in a few months vs 2 years unless they ask. 4. Even when using AI, keep your hands-on skill warm. Most companies still do old-school leetcode interviews. 5. As an extreme backup this might even become something you monetize yourself. Hope this helps, and all the best!
comments.author: keeda

comments.text: Obv take all of the below with a grain of salt. This is based on my experience as a 50+ dev. YMMV > I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) My controversial take is: build something using AI in a language you have no clue about. I did exactly this, and it was the fastest way to level up at the one skill everyone wants today. Don't even use a text editor. Make every change via AI. It is the purest way to find all the annoying parts and get better at it. Your lazy engineer brain will find new ways to avoid the pain and be lazy and that is where the gold is. If you can, join a company (any company) at a much reduced rate and give yourself a year to fully learn how to build everything in AI. If you can find a company that uses a language and tech stack you know nothing about even better. Give it a year of retraining and then go back out for the high paying role in a large company with this pure AI experience under your belt. The folks who say that working with AI is not a specialized skill have no idea what they are talking about. Also a course like mega.dev is also very useful to re-ground in the new ways.

comments.text: Here's how my friend solved almost an exact same problem and leveraged me to do it. A very close friend of mine was in a similar situation. He was laid off at Tesla and then took six months just to recover only to find out that gap in his resume met a wall with every recruiter conversation he had. At the time I was running a company (Prebacked, roughly a startup accelerator). You're making a good deal of noise, but not a good deal of money. Jeff (not real name) called me up and said "I'm coming to work for you". I told him I would love that and needed all the help I could get, but had no money to pay him. He offered to work for free for a time. He said, "I'm going to work my ass off for you, and I'm going to do a great job. And when I do, you're going to give me a kick-ass reference when I go job hunting." He did work his ass off. He did do a great job. He met some folks at our program and helped with a cool contracting project with Google, and he flipped that experience and my referral into employment at Apple, where he's been making a killer salary ever since. There are a lot, lot of people who could use your help (many on HN!) but not be able to afford it. You need references and a closed gap, they need SWE help. Go do a project. If you think a trade like that might help you get on your feet, please DM me. I'm one of those. I also have been told my network is... rather elite, if if not me then I could think of probably 100 people who could.

comments.text: Tap your connections. I recently started a job after 1 year unemployment from layoffs. I put out a bit over 400 applications, and the one that finally got me a job was a referral. Are you connected on linkedin (it sucks, but you have to deal with it) to all of your former coworkers? From every past job? Reach out to any of them who you think would recognize your face. Also, don't quit. The move when you find out layoffs are coming is to start looking for a job. Make them fire you or lay you off. There's no reason to quit ahead of time. It likely makes you ineligible for unemployment, and forfeits any severance. As for what to say about the gap on your resume, you can honestly say the company did layoffs. It isn't the whole truth, but it is true.

comments.text: Firstly, I deeply empathize with your situation and its important to note the market is historically really bad for everyone right now. After 15 years of experience, you should have people you can instantly call who can get you interviews or even direct jobs at the place they are working. The idea of applying to jobs after 10 years of experience is very futile. At that point, your network and industry reputation gets you directly placed. Your peers (the people you started your career with) with the same YOE are in hiring/leadership roles now like head of engineering, VP, Staff Engineer etc. so calling them and asking to be directly placed is the way.

comments.text: Same here until recently. I finally landed at a startup that one of my old coworkers was at. I think the gap actually helped me on the job, as everything AI is completely new to me and I'm not having to unlearn last year's AI lessons. On the job, AI is all that matters. I have zero go experience, have not typed a character into an IDE, and still couldn't write a "hello world" or even define a function myself, but I'm the top contributor in the company every month I've been here. (I can read and understand go, and smell when things don't seem quite right, and have 20 years of architect experience to fall back on though). So I guess the point is, don't feel like the gap is prohibitive. It may make it harder to land an interview, but you should be prepared to justify that it won't make you less valuable, and plausibly the opposite.

posts.title: Tell HN: OpenRouter prompts to Minimax may have been read
posts.text: I received the following email from OpenRouter and it appears authentic. posts.title: Ask HN: Should Uber Ratings Decay over Time?
posts.text: I’ve been thinking about how platforms like Uber calculate reputation scores, and I believe there’s a fundamental flaw in how historical ratings are treated. Uber calculates passenger ratings using the last 500 rated trips, regardless of when those trips occurred. In my case, I have 455 ratings, 426 of which are five stars (93.6%). My overall rating is 4.86. What bothers me isn’t the score itself, but the underlying methodology. A negative rating from five years ago can carry exactly the same weight as one received yesterday. And if you’re an infrequent user who hasn’t accumulated 500 ratings, that negative feedback could influence your reputation for years. This raises an interesting question: Should reputation systems measure your historical average, or should they attempt to represent who you are today? One possible solution is exponential time decay: Weight = 2^(-t/H) Where t is the age of the rating and H is a half-life, perhaps 12 months. Under that approach, a rating from one year ago would carry 50% of its original weight, and one from two years ago just 25%. Of course, this introduces other challenges. How do you prevent someone with a history of poor behaviour from simply waiting for their reputation to recover? How do you maintain statistical confidence for infrequent users? Would Bayesian smoothing or a minimum effective sample size help? There’s also a broader philosophical question around the right to be forgotten. Should digital reputation systems indefinitely preserve the consequences of historical assessments, particularly when those assessments are subjective and potentially no longer representative? I’m curious how others would approach this. * Is a rolling window of 500 ratings statistically defensible without considering time? * Would exponential decay produce a fairer and more predictive reputation score? * Should platforms expose both a lifetime rating and a recent-behaviour rating? * Are there better approaches already being used in other reputation systems? I’d be particularly interested in perspectives from people who’ve worked on marketplace ranking, trust and safety, or reputation algorithms. It seems like a relatively simple mathematical change, but one with potentially significant implications for fairness across digital platforms.

It's primary purpose is for live boxscores because all of the major sports sites have terrible UI/UX experiences. I always defaulted to ESPN.com but it's so slow and awful. Center Court is basically a bridge between espn.com (or nba.com) and more advanced stat focused sites that don't offer a good live experience. Instead of storing computed statistics in a database, I store raw play by play payloads immutability and everything else is derived from those and can be trivially rebuilt so the event log is a derived cache of the payloads. Every stat on every page is a pure fold over the event log at request time; no derived number is stored. This enables some powerful features like being able to re-derive a game's entire state at any point of the game (or even a time range). Same with fan games, ROM hacks, mods, homebrew titles and recomps. AI has led to a huge flood of them to the point it's almost impossible to know what's human made or not anymore. I suspect that's going to happen to every industry where programming plays even a minor role. Content Management Systems? There will be thousands of options available. Messaging tools? Thousands of options. Image editors, text editors, wiki software and office software? Again, thousands of options available. The positive side is that anyone can compete with just about any company in any tech related industry. The negative side is that most of these people and companies will have no idea what they're doing, or give up and move on within a week or two. Lots of industries will probably outright crash due to the flood of competition making supply outstrip demand a thousand to one, and a lot of unfortunate people and organisations will end up losing their work/livelihood/home/etc when the vibe-coded tools they attempt to use end up being full of bugs and oversights. RIP anyone who puts their faith in tax audit software for instance. An awful lot of software development houses and sub-industries are probably on the way out too. WordPress development agencies and other CMS specific outlets (like those focused on Shopify, Magento, Moodle, Drupal, etc) are going to find a larger and larger percentage of their customers asking AI to build or maintain their sites rather than them. The market for brochure and CRUD sites for small and medium sized businesses will probably crater. The ability to use AI to replace a team with one or two people means the job market is probably getting even worse than it is now. AI is going to destroy the bottom 60-70% of programming jobs, and that percentage is only going up in future. Your choices are basically to either hope you can be in the top 10% or so of software engineers and make enough money to retire before things get truly dire, to hope you can start an SaaS company/do freelance work, or to find another line of work altogether. It's probably not going to be any better for designers, writers or other office employees either. But yeah, my prediction is that markets will get flooded with (often low-quality ) software, lots of existing companies and jobs will go away, and only the most technically skilled programmers will be hireable in the next decade.

comments.text: Desire for software is kind of a fractal. Take a word processor. I want a word processor. OK, here's Microsoft Word. Well, I want it to be better at writing math than that. Well, here's an add-on (at least, back in the day that's how it was done). Well, the add-on's nice, but I want it to work a bit differently... And so it goes, more and more specific desires, with fewer and fewer people that want those specific desires. So one possible future is that we move further out on the fractal. More people get what they want, even if not many people want the same thing. This means that the customizations have to take less software engineer time, because a customer base of just a few people can't pay very much. In that future, the key activity is going to be efficiently finding small groups of users, learning what they actually want, and then generating that.

posts.title: Ask HN: Why no AI-led memory vulns in Python?
posts.text: Python usually means CPython, which means C. Most AI-led vulnerabilities lately have been memory mismanagement - what is keeping Python isolated if it is written in C?

comments.text: Well, it might just be a matter of time. We've already had serious issues in Ruby with both string case conversion ( https://verialabs.com/ruby2shell/ ) and the regex engine (e.g. https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/news/2026/10/23/regexp-fixes-fo... ). And there have been attempts at fuzzing Python that have found real issues, apparently just not on the same scale (e.g. https://github.com/Broyojo/python-formalization ). A couple of things I can think of: first, the model for interfacing to "compiled code" — both C extensions, and compiled Python bytecode — isn't expected to be secure anyway, and never has been. You can trivially wrap a garbage `bytes` in a `code` object, execute it and get a segfault; and you can trivially use the `ctypes` API to corrupt memory. Second, the normal use paths are well-tested and bottom out in an interpretation layer that isn't very well optimized because of how much dynamic nonsense it has to support (even beyond other languages in its class like Ruby). On the other hand, the bytecode format tends to change with almost every "minor" release (i.e. annually now). There's probably plenty of room for a mistake in that churn.

comments.text: There are two issues: 1) transitioning your skills, and 2) persuading someone to hire/pay you for your new skills. Transitioning your skills is possible. But embedded is a different world and a different mindset. You a lot less RAM and a smaller CPU. You may have hard deadlines - the right answer can be wrong if it's too late. You may have multiple threads that have to share data and not corrupt it, no matter what order events occur in. In the worst case, you may not have logging available at all, and you may not have a debugger. (I think the worst I ever had to do was attach a logic analyzer to the address bus, triggered by a specific address, and then use it to look at past memory addresses in order to figure out what path of execution had got me to the point of the crash.) So, yeah. It's a different world. Learnable, but different. Getting someone to believe you can do it enough that they're willing to pay you: I don't have great advice there. I spent almost my whole career in embedded. It seems to me that it's easier to get from there into, say, desktop programming, than it is to go the other way. Your best bet might be to emphasize your native development background, and count on there being a shortage of embedded people.
